claims.text: The selected alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy containing five nearly equiatomic transition metals.
The selected alloy's superconducting behavior is uncharacterized.
Random multi-element occupation creates local lattice distortions in the alloy.
The local lattice distortions stabilize a uniform electronic density of states.
High configurational entropy and its local structural fluctuations enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling produces isotropic conventional s-wave Cooper pairing despite compositional disorder.
Removing one principal element reduces the alloy's configurational entropy.
A principal element can be removed while retaining the same BCC phase and overall structure.
Reducing configurational entropy weakens favorable local fluctuations and disrupts the local environments responsible for superconductivity.
The full high-entropy alloy will undergo a sharp superconducting transition within 2–20 K at ambient pressure.
The superconducting transition of the full alloy will be evidenced by zero electrical resistance and a diamagnetic response.
Relative to the full alloy, the reduced-entropy variant will have a lower Tc, a broader or incomplete transition, or no superconductivity.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single stable BCC phase.
High pressure, a different crystallographic phase, or extreme compositional deviations may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Four-probe resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and heat capacity can be used together to characterize the superconducting transition.
Failure of element removal to cause a significant change in Tc, transition width, or superconducting completeness would falsify the proposed entropy-controlled mechanism.
